title: Linux Kernel Developers Consider Adding Agents.md to Help Guide AI/LLM Agents
content:
Linux Kernel Developers Consider Adding AGENTS.md To Help Guide AI/LLM Agents
While the Linux kernel continues to be bombarded with patches from AI/LLM agents, to date the kernel hasn't carried an AGENTS.md Markdown file with instructions catering to AI/LLM agents. But a patch set out today would finally introduce one.
Longtime Linux developer Sasha Levin who has worked on other AI initiatives for the kernel like helping to determine patches for back-porting to the stable kernel tree and AI-powered merge conflict resolution is now looking to add an AGENTS.md to the kernel source tree.
The proposed AGENTS.md is just linking to the Linux kernel's README file. From there it points to documentation on coding assistants and other information relevant to kernel developers.
The rationale for adding AGENTS.md to the Linux kernel tree is that in testing on one AI agent without the file, the AI agent added a "Signed-off-by" tag to the proposed kernel patch even though it shouldn't have without the user explicitly signing off on their own. It also resorted to its own attribution tag rather than the kernel standardized Assisted-by tag.
Testing on a second unnamed AI agent without AGENTS.md added no attributions. But after adding the AGENTS.md, both agents behaved to kernel standards and the second one better conformed to the kernel development best practices.
This kernel mailing list thread laid out the patch proposing the AGENTS.md introduction. While it's just linking to the README flle, not all are in favor at this point. There have been some objections on the LKML to the patch given that making AI/LLMs consume the entire Linux kernel README and associated documentation would increase token consumption. More catered documentation most relevant to AI/LLMs would be one way to help reduce token consumption, but we'll see what comes of this new Linux kernel proposal around enhancing AI workflows.

report.summary: Linux kernel developers are considering a patch that adds an AGENTS.md file to the source tree to steer AI/LLM coding agents toward kernel patch conventions.
report.background: AI coding agents are now submitting a steady stream of patches to the Linux kernel mailing list, and maintainers have been struggling with submissions that look plausible but violate long-standing conventions. Agentic tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor increasingly look for project-local instruction files (commonly AGENTS.md) to learn a repository's rules before editing code. The Linux kernel has so far carried no such file, leaving agents to guess at conventions like attribution tags and sign-off rules. Sasha Levin, a longtime kernel developer already working on AI-assisted stable backporting and merge-conflict resolution, has proposed adding a minimal AGENTS.md that simply points to the kernel's existing README and coding-assistant documentation.
key_points: Sasha Levin's patch adds an AGENTS.md to the Linux kernel tree that merely links to the existing README and the kernel's documentation on coding assistants, rather than duplicating rules. The goal is a single, predictable entry point that AI agents can read before proposing kernel patches.

In testing, one unnamed AI agent given no AGENTS.md wrongly added a 'Signed-off-by' tag, which legally implies a human developer's certification, and invented its own attribution tag instead of using the kernel's standardized 'Assisted-by' tag.

A second agent added no attribution at all without the file. After AGENTS.md was present, both agents followed kernel standards, and the second one aligned noticeably better with kernel development best practices.

The proposal is not unanimous. Some LKML reviewers object that pointing agents at the entire kernel README plus linked documentation would burn large numbers of tokens, and argue for more targeted, AI-specific instructions instead.

The debate sits inside a wider trend: AI/LLM agents are flooding kernel mailing lists with patches, pushing maintainers to formalize machine-readable contribution rules the same way they do for human contributors.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is an early sign that major open-source projects will treat agent instruction files as part of their public interface, not an afterthought. If the kernel adopts AGENTS.md, it validates a convention that tool builders can standardize on, and it creates pressure for agents to respect project-specific attribution, licensing and sign-off semantics. For developers, it means less time cleaning up plausible-but-wrong AI patches and clearer signals about what agents may and may not do autonomously. For regular users, the practical effect is indirect but real: fewer malformed patches reaching stable kernels, and a clearer audit trail distinguishing human-authored work from machine assistance.
report.tools: Watch the AGENTS.md convention itself and how Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor and Aider consume it. For kernel work, follow the kernel's Documentation on coding assistants, the b4 patch tool, and Levin's AI backporting and merge-conflict tooling. Anyone experimenting locally can add an AGENTS.md to their own repo, compare it against CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md and .cursorrules, and measure token cost versus instruction quality.
